Introduction

I came across an article that gives a short history of acoustics, and it ties in closely with several of my earlier pieces. So I have embellished it a little and present it here as a timeline. Obviously it covers only one small corner of the history of acoustics, so after the shameless word “complete” I have added “very brief” as a show of humility.

1861

The German scientist Johann Philipp Reis invents the microphone, and the loudspeaker along with it: one device, two uses. Both are later steadily improved by Alexander Graham Bell (the Bell of Bell Labs) and Ernst Siemens (the founder of Siemens).

Ah, a good excuse to open with the short film my PhD institute made last year. The venerable Mr. Reis travels 160 years through time to visit my old professor…

1863

Hermann von Helmholtz publishes On the Sensations of Tone as a Physiological Basis for the Theory of Music. The book describes the Helmholtz resonator, which uses the air in a cavity to amplify sound at one particular frequency (much like blowing across an empty bottle). Helmholtz used his resonators to pick out the individual tones in the sounds of musical instruments.

Hey, little conch, why do you sound like the sea?

1877

The Theory of Sound is published in Britain. Its author, Lord Rayleigh, would win the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1904. Rayleigh discovered the Rayleigh wave, a sound wave that travels along the surface of a solid. The rayl, the unit of acoustic impedance, is named after him.

1883

Krakatoa erupts in Indonesia, producing what is considered the loudest sound in modern human history. Some 36,000 people die in the tsunamis triggered by the eruption, the shock waves keep going for days afterward, and the Earth’s climate is affected for years.

The loudest sound ever on Earth is said to be the Chicxulub impact. The asteroid struck with two million times the energy of the Tsar Bomba and changed both the Earth’s rotation and its orbit. How many decibels was it? Supposedly only the dinosaurs know. But were there even decibels back then?

1924

No, there weren’t. Nobody knew what a decibel was until 1924, when the concept was introduced by Bell Labs. I covered the decibel in detail in an earlier article, so I won’t repeat it here. Click below 👇

What on earth is a decibel, and why 1 + 1 ≠ 2

1930

The International Electrotechnical Commission officially drops “cycles per second” and adopts the hertz as the unit of frequency, in honor of Heinrich Hertz. Hertz’s nephew, Gustav Ludwig Hertz, later became director of a Siemens research laboratory.

1930

The Perrin acoustic array makes the cover of a magazine. The array was invented by the French Nobel laureate Jean-Baptiste Perrin, and the description at the time read: “Airplane Finder Which Locates Ships in Flight, and Registers Their Altitude, Speed and Distance from the Apparatus.” In other words, it could find aircraft and determine their altitude, speed and distance from the device. This is the ancestor of the modern microphone array. In its day it was high tech: a microphone array several times taller than a person. Decades of evolution later, microphone arrays are everyday items, built into hundreds of millions of smart speakers, phones and earphones.

A history of acoustics: sound visualization, part 1

A history of acoustics: sound visualization, part 2

The core purpose of the array, localization, has not changed. What has changed is that, thanks to advances in technology, arrays can now make sound visible.

1933

Anyone who knows a little acoustics will recognize the equal-loudness contours below. Each blue curve shows, for one perceived loudness, the actual sound pressure level needed at each frequency.

Two years ago I wrote at length about psychoacoustics. If you’d like to know more, click away 👇

A history of acoustics: psychoacoustics, part 1

A history of acoustics: psychoacoustics, part 2

1936

The A-weighting curve becomes a standard. A-weighting is another correction that accounts for the characteristics of human hearing. The curve peaks at around 2000 Hz, the frequency region where the ear is most sensitive, but at 20 Hz the ear is very insensitive. In the figure, 20 Hz corresponds to −50 dB. That means two sounds at the same sound pressure level, one at 2000 Hz and one at 20 Hz, are perceived as differing by 50 dB in loudness.

1936

Stanley Smith Stevens of Harvard University proposes the sone as the unit of loudness. The word comes from the Latin sonus, meaning sound. Stevens also founded Harvard’s Psycho-Acoustic Laboratory.

Stanley Smith Stevens (1906–1973)

1942

Leo Beranek of Harvard, who can fairly be called the father of American acoustics, builds the first anechoic chamber. A (fully) anechoic chamber simulates an acoustic free field; later came the hemi-anechoic chamber, which simulates a half free field. The chamber was built to test loudspeakers for the US Air Force. War really is the prime mover of scientific and technological progress.

Beranek also defined the Articulation Index (AI, and no, not artificial intelligence), which describes how well speech can be understood against background noise. The AI was used to judge whether pilots wearing different models of headset could clearly hear instructions from the ground.

Fully anechoic chamber

Hemi-anechoic chamber

1961

Professor Karl Eberhard Zwicker in Munich proposes the Bark scale, which later becomes a standard. The Bark is the unit of the critical band. Put simply, there are 24 places on the basilar membrane of the cochlea that resonate most strongly at 24 different frequencies, which divides the audible range of 20 Hz–22 kHz into 24 bands: the critical bands. I covered this in some detail in my earlier history of psychoacoustics, so I won’t belabor it here. The critical bands get wider as frequency rises.

1963

The internet is invented by an acoustician, J.C.R. Licklider. Licklider was a researcher in the US Department of Defense at the Pentagon. He secured funding for his office and began building the “Intergalactic Computer Network,” which became today’s internet. Licklider has been credited with three great inventions: computer science programs at several leading American universities, time-sharing, and networking.

1975

The calculation of loudness becomes the international standard ISO 532. It has two methods: a narrow-band spectral approach and a 1/3-octave approach. The standard also takes into account the masking effects described by Zwicker.

1981

The ECMA-74 standard, “Measurement of Airborne Noise emitted by Information Technology and Telecommunications Equipment,” is published. It includes methods for calculating the tone-to-noise ratio and the prominence ratio. A pure tone must be at least 8 dB above its masking noise to be heard.

1990

The bible of psychoacoustics, Psychoacoustics: Facts and Models, is published, by Eberhard Zwicker and Hugo Fastl of the Technical University of Munich.

1994

A sensor that measures acoustic particle velocity in air appears.

The Microflown particle velocity sensor

Particle velocity: there’s more to sound than pressure

2000

The Council of the European Union adopts Directive 2000/14/EC, the Outdoor Noise Directive (OND). In the member states, 57 types of outdoor equipment are now required to meet noise emission limits. From then on, sound power became familiar to the general public, for example from the energy label (anyone who has lived in Europe will have seen one).

2018

ECMA-74 adds a method for calculating tonality in Annex G.

2020–2021

Variations on a coronavirus…
